title: I made three AI seats argue over the spec before any code. Here's what 10 runs showed.
summary:
Most of the bad code I've gotten from coding agents wasn't badly written. It was the right code for the wrong plan. The agent misread the task, assumed something about the repo that wasn't true, and then executed that assumption very well.

So I built a tool that spends its effort before the code. It's called Open Council. Three seats argue over a PRD until they all sign off on the same document:

  • Lead PM writes the brief and the PRD.
  • Chief Engineer checks every claim against the real code. Every objection has to cite a file:line.
  • Chief Architect rules on deadlocks and reviews the agreed document. It runs with no tools, so it judges the text, not the repo.

When all three sign off, I approve the PRD with a token. Only then does the Engineer implement it, in an isolated clone. The harness runs the project's gates (its real test commands) and opens a PR only if they pass. Anything else ends as BLOCKED or STALLED, never DONE.

Last week I had ten councils run on version 0.2.1 to see how this holds up. Here's what happened, including the parts that didn't work.

The setup

All ten ran in solo mode, which means every seat is Claude Code (Lead PM on Sonnet, Chief Engineer on Opus, Chief Architect on Sonnet with tools off). They used the quick profile, with at most 4 rounds. The targets were local copies of two small repos: a toy slugify library I keep for testing, and Open Council itself. Local copies have no GitHub remote, so no run could open a PR. That last step ends BLOCKED by design.

# Task Outcome Rounds Minutes
1 slugify: empty string + accents signed off, gate passed 4 6.6
2 gates --json signed off, gate passed 4 6.8
3 gate recipes for Python, Go, Rust signed off, gate passed 3 7.3
4 slugify: maxLength STALLED 4 6.2
5 slugify: empty + accents (repeat) signed off, gate passed 3 4.2
6 gates --json (repeat) STALLED 4 7.2
7 slugify: ß ø æ œ đ ł þ signed off, gate failed, BLOCKED 2 3.4
8 slugify: maxLength (repeat) signed off, gate passed 4 6.3
9 gate recipes (repeat) signed off, gate passed 4 9.2
10 slugify: empty + accents (repeat) signed off, gate passed 2 3.1

8 of 10 signed off. 7 of those 8 passed their gate. The median time to a sign-off or a stall was 6.5 minutes.

The catch nobody asked for

Six of the runs were on the slugify repo. In all six, the Chief Engineer's first objection had nothing to do with the task.

The repo's package.json had "test": "node --test test/". On Node 22 that argument is read as a module path, not a folder, so npm test ran 0 of the 2 existing tests. It had been quietly broken since before I started. No task mentioned it.

In run 1 the Engineer reproduced it, tried two working alternatives, and made fixing the test script the first commit of the plan. Its reasoning was simple: you can't claim the new tests pass if the runner doesn't run tests.

This is the thing I wanted from the design. A single agent asked to "handle empty strings in slugify" would most likely write the fix and the tests and report that they pass. A seat whose only job is to check claims against the repo found that the claim couldn't be checked at all.

What went wrong

Two runs stalled, and the same way. In both, the Engineer had no objections left. Then the Architect raised one more concern. In run 4 it asked for a README line the task never mentioned. The revision that answered it introduced a new problem: one of the new assertions would fail on a correct implementation. The Engineer objected in the last round, the budget ran out, and nothing reached me for approval. The harness wrote the last draft and the open objections to a file and stopped.

A stall is the system working, because nothing wrong got built. But two stalls with the same shape tell me the Architect's late concerns cost more than they're worth. I already made one change for this: a concern that could have been raised in an earlier round is waived on a resubmission. These two runs show it isn't enough yet.

One run was blocked by its own plan. In run 7 the council agreed on a plan and named its own test command, node --test test/slug.test.js. But the project config runs npm test, which was still broken in that repo, and the Architect had ruled that fixing package.json was out of scope. So execution ran the configured gate, it failed, and the run ended BLOCKED. Nothing was pushed. The code itself passed the plan's own 7 tests when I checked afterwards.

The harness did the right thing by not calling it done. The real bug is that a PRD can name a gate the project doesn't run, and nothing flags that before execution. That's an open issue now.

Solo mode isn't the real test. Every seat in these runs was the same model family. The point of separate seats is that they don't share blind spots, and the council is designed to put Claude, Gemini and Grok in different seats. I haven't run that mixed setup enough to say whether it catches more. Ten runs on two small repos, with three tasks repeated, is a smoke test, not a rate.

What I took from it

  1. Review the plan, not just the diff. The most useful objection in these runs was about the repo's state, not the task. It only came up because a seat was told to check claims against the code before anyone wrote any.
  2. Make "done" something the harness checks, not something the agent says. Run 7 had passing code and still ended BLOCKED, because the gate the project actually runs failed. I'd rather read a BLOCKED than find out later.
  3. Publish the failures. The stalls taught me more than the sign-offs, and they're the part I'd want to see before trusting a tool like this.

Trying it

You need Node 18 or later, macOS or Linux, and Claude Code. In a git repo:

npm install -g open-council-cli
council init --solo
council doctor
council backlog add "your task here" --priority 1
SESSION=$(council open my-task --item 001)
council deliberate "$SESSION"

When it signs off, it prints the PRD's path and the exact council approve command. That step is yours to run. Then council handoff "$SESSION" and council run "$SESSION" implement it and open the PR.

The code, and full replays of these runs with every objection, are at https://github.com/goshtasb/OpenCouncil. It's MIT licensed. If you run a council and it stalls or ships something wrong, that's the report I'd most like to read.

This article was written with the help of AI, and the ten runs were driven by an AI agent on my behalf. I checked the numbers against the run logs before publishing.

title: The Pragmatic 3-Step Roadmap to UBI: Start by Doubling Rural Pensions and Universal Child Allowances
summary:
Whenever we discuss Universal Basic Income (UBI) in the age of AI, the most common objection in the comments is always the same:

"The philosophy sounds great, but paying 1.4 billion people even a modest monthly stipend would cost trillions! Where does the money come from? If we can't fund full universal coverage tomorrow morning, isn't UBI just a utopian daydream?"

This objection sounds hard-headed, but it commits a classic all-or-nothing engineering fallacy.

Look back at the history of modern social contracts over the past two centuries—whether universal public education in the 19th century or social security and universal healthcare in the 20th. Not a single transformative social safety net launched on Day One with 100% population coverage and 100% payout levels. Every one of them followed a staged engineering rollout: starting with the most vulnerable groups where marginal utility and social consensus were highest, proving the fiscal multiplier, and then scaling to universal coverage as industrial productivity surged.

As AI agents and humanoid robots rapidly automate cognitive and physical labor in 2026, abundant productivity must translate into human freedom and dignity, not existential fear. We do not need to wait a decade for an overnight miracle. We can launch a crystal-clear, fiscally grounded 3-Step UBI Engineering Roadmap today.

Step 1 (Immediate Launch): Double Rural Basic Pensions and Issue Unconditional Monthly Child Allowances

Why must Phase 1 target seniors and young children first?

Because every dollar invested at the two ends of the human lifecycle delivers an immediate macroeconomic multiplier while relieving the heaviest financial pressure on working-age families—with zero ideological debate about "discouraging work." A 70-year-old rural farmer and a 3-year-old toddler should never be forced to compete in the labor market.

Let's run the exact fiscal math:

1. Raise Rural and Non-Working Basic Pensions from ~200 RMB to 800–1,000 RMB/Month

Roughly 170 million seniors in China—mostly rural parents who built the nation's agricultural and industrial foundation—currently receive a baseline pension of only 150 to 250 RMB per month.

  • Raising their unconditional baseline pension by 600 RMB per month requires an annual outlay of roughly 1.22 trillion RMB (less than 1% of national GDP), easily funded by transferring state-owned capital dividends and early AI infrastructure taxes.
  • The Multiplier Effect: Low-income seniors have a marginal propensity to consume above 0.85. Nearly every yuan flows immediately into local groceries, healthcare, and household goods, while lifting a massive financial and emotional burden off hundreds of millions of working-age children.

2. An Unconditional 800 RMB/Month Child Allowance for Every Child Aged 0–6

With roughly 75 million children under age six, issuing an automatic, means-test-free 800 RMB monthly child allowance directly to mothers costs roughly 720 billion RMB per year.

  • Combined, protecting both seniors and young children requires under 2 trillion RMB annually—a fraction of traditional infrastructure stimulus, yet infinitely more effective at reviving household consumption confidence.

Step 2 (Years 3–5): Launch the "Youth AI Transition & Creator Basic Stipend"

Once the household floor for seniors and children is secured, Phase 2 addresses the demographic hit hardest by white-collar and factory automation: working-age adults aged 22 to 45.

Traditional unemployment insurance suffers from a fatal design flaw known as the welfare cliff: the moment an unemployed worker earns a few hundred dollars driving a gig car or building an indie app, their benefits are cut off. This traps people in short-term survival anxiety instead of allowing them to reskill.

Phase 2 replaces punitive unemployment insurance with an unconditional AI Transition & Creator Stipend:

  1. No Welfare Cliff: Workers in structurally automating sectors receive a baseline 1,500–2,000 RMB monthly floor that does not vanish when they earn side income building AI products, teaching, or creating art.
  2. Universal Compute Vouchers: Alongside cash, every citizen receives a monthly quota of public frontier AI tokens and cloud compute—ensuring that the tools of AI creation belong to everyone, not just tech monopolies.

Step 3 (Years 5–10): Merge into Full Universal Compute & Automation Dividends (Full UBI)

As humanoid robots scale across manufacturing, agriculture, and construction, and AI agents handle 80% of routine cognitive workflows, the marginal cost of physical goods and digital services will plummet toward zero.

At that point, the direct digital disbursement rails and sovereign dividend pools built in Steps 1 and 2 seamlessly expand into Full Universal Basic Income:

  • Self-Sustaining Sovereign Pool: A 2% to 5% Automation & Token Dividend Tax on commercial compute clusters and autonomous robotic fleets funds the national dividend pool.
  • Survival Decoupled from Labor: Every citizen receives a lifelong monthly dividend guaranteeing housing, nutrition, healthcare, and creative freedom as a birthright.

Conclusion: A Bridge to the Stars Is Built One Brick at a Time

Never let the difficulty of Step 3 become an excuse to delay Step 1. Doubling the pensions of elderly parents and issuing unconditional child allowances today is the first concrete brick of the AI century's new social contract.

title: Claude Code forgets everything when you close it. Here's how I made it remember (and share it with Claude.ai)
summary:
Every morning I opened Claude Code and did the same thing: explained my project again. What we changed yesterday. Why we picked that approach. What was still broken.

Then I'd switch to Claude.ai on my phone, or hand a task to Codex, and do it all over again.

The worst part wasn't repeating myself. It was the AI forgetting why we made a decision, and quietly undoing a fix from two days ago.

So I built a small open-source tool to fix it for myself: CogniCore. This post shows how it works and how to set it up in a couple of minutes.

What actually gets lost between sessions

When a Claude Code session ends, the useful parts are gone:

the goal you were working toward
decisions, and the reason behind each one
open tasks you left for later
exact values: ticket IDs, versions, file paths, ports

A CLAUDE.md file helps, but you have to remember to update it, it keeps growing, and Claude.ai or ChatGPT can't read a file on your laptop.

The idea: a handoff, saved automatically

CogniCore uses Claude Code's hooks. After each turn it saves a short, structured handoff:

text
Goal: Make the deploy pipeline survive restarts
State: PR #193 merged, downtime 27 min -> 6 s
Decisions:

  • Uploads run in a background process (why: a turn never waits on the network) Open tasks:
  • Publish the next release to PyPI Values: fix/deploy-permissions, port 8765

When the next session starts, it injects a short brief (about 450 tokens) instead of the whole history. If the agent needs more, it asks for a specific section.

Two design choices I'm happy with:

Rule-based extraction by default. It only calls an LLM to compress a session when it's over 3,000 tokens, so most saves cost zero model calls and memory is ready in about a second.
Newest revision wins. Uploads run in the background, and an older upload can never overwrite newer work.
Setup (about 2 minutes)
bash
pipx install "cognicore-env[mcp]"
cognicore install # sets up Claude Code and Codex

Restart Claude Code. That's it for local memory. Nothing leaves your machine.

Want the same memory in Claude.ai, ChatGPT or Cursor? Turn on sync:

bash
cognicore login

Then add the CogniCore connector in Claude.ai. Only the short handoff is synced, never your transcripts or file contents.

The test that convinced me

In Claude Code, I asked it to remember a code word: BLUE-HERON-4417.

The next day, in a separate Claude.ai chat, I asked: "What did I just do in Claude Code?"

It told me what I'd worked on, and gave me the code word back.

How it compares

I benchmarked it against claude-mem 15.7.0, the most popular memory plugin, on the same tasks. Both finished every follow-up correctly. CogniCore used 53K-60K new tokens vs 147K-216K, and memory was ready in about 1 second vs 70-130 seconds.

It's my own benchmark, so be skeptical: the script (scripts/bench_realworld.py) is in the repo and I'd genuinely like to hear if you get different numbers.

What's still not great
On Claude.ai, memory only updates when Claude decides to call the tool. There are no hooks on the web.
The saved summaries are sometimes noisy. I'm improving the extraction every week.
Try it

It's free and open source (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/cognicore-dev/cognicore-env

CogniCore — Memory that follows you between AI apps

CogniCore gives Claude, ChatGPT and coding agents like Claude Code and Codex a shared memory, so every new chat picks up where the last one stopped.

claudepluginhub.com

mcp.market

How do you keep context when you switch between AI tools? A notes file, copy-paste, or just re-explaining? I'd love to hear what works for you.

title: I Ran the Same Coding Task Through 3 Local LLMs — the Free One on My Laptop Won Twice
summary:
I spent a Saturday afternoon doing something deeply unproductive on paper: I ran the same three coding tasks through three local models on my own laptop, and timed everything. No cloud, no API key, no subscription. Just a mid-range machine, a fan that sounded like a hairdryer, and a spreadsheet.
The question I actually wanted answered: can a free model sitting on your own disk do real work, or is local AI still a toy you show your friends?

The setup

Three models, all open-weight, all run through Ollama on the same laptop (16GB RAM, no dedicated GPU — the machine I actually own, not the one in a benchmark blog post):

  • A 7B general coding model
  • A 14B model, the biggest that fits without the laptop giving up

title: 5 Python PDF libraries vs 1,068 broken PDFs: what crashed, and why one of my explanations was wrong
summary:
I fed 1,068 broken PDFs to five Python libraries and asked each one for the text. The files are Mozilla's pdf.js test suite: PDFs people attached to bug reports over the years, with broken cross-reference tables, strange fonts and fuzzed bytes. If your code reads PDFs that strangers upload, these are the files that will eventually reach it.

Library Failed* Failed where 3+ others worked Total time Slowest file
PyMuPDF 2.1 5 2 14 s 5.9 s
pypdfium2 5.14.0 14 2 6 s 0.6 s
pypdf 6.21.4 23 7 83 s 13.8 s
pdfminer.six 20260107 22 6 204 s timeout (60 s)
pdfplumber 0.11.10 23 7 225 s timeout (60 s)

* Raised an error or hit the 60-second limit. Not counted: 12 password-protected files that at least two libraries reported as needing a password. Python 3.13, 2-vCPU ARM server, each library in its own worker processes.

The fast two are 6 to 40 times faster

pypdfium2 got through all 1,068 files in 6 seconds. PyMuPDF needed 14. pypdf took 83, pdfminer.six 204, and pdfplumber 225, which is almost four minutes for the same pile.

pdfplumber's worst file was freeculture.pdf, a 352-page book. It hit my 60-second limit, while pdfminer.six, the parser pdfplumber is built on, reads the same book in about 12 seconds. So the time goes into pdfplumber's own layout work. If you only need the text, you don't need pdfplumber.

pdfplumber is not a fallback for pdfminer.six

Five of their unique failures are the same files, often with the same error ('PDFObjRef' object is not subscriptable). That makes sense once you know pdfplumber uses pdfminer.six to parse. If you want a second library to catch what the first one drops, pick one with a different parser.

pypdfium2 is the easiest one to build a fallback around. 22 of its 24 failures happen right when it opens the file ("Data format error"), so you find out at once and can hand the file to something else.

The π file, and the explanation I had to take back

pdf.js has a test file, filled-background.pdf, stuffed with 100,000-digit numbers: π, in three objects and again in a comment inside the cross-reference table. pypdf stops with LimitReachedError (it refuses numbers longer than 64 characters). The other four libraries read it.

My first write-up said the comment alone was the culprit. While preparing this post I tested that, by deleting the comment line. pypdf still failed with the same error. Shortening every digit run turned it into a different error from the same xref parser. So this file trips pypdf in more than one way, and my neat one-line cause was wrong. I've fixed the original note.

The other lesson from this run was about timeouts. An earlier harness of mine used a Python alarm signal to stop slow files. One file sat inside C code for 44 minutes and the alarm never fired. Now every library runs in a worker process that gets killed from outside.

Only one readable file beat all five libraries: poppler-742-0-fuzzed.pdf. Five more failed everywhere, but they're encrypted.

This only says whether a library breaks, not how good its text is. Reading order, spacing and tables are a separate test. About 350 to 390 files gave no text in every library, mostly because they hold only images or shapes. And check the licences: PyMuPDF is AGPL or commercial, the other four are permissive.

Run it yourself

The harness is corpusdiff, a small open-source tool I wrote for this kind of test:

git clone https://github.com/prometheus-maker/corpusdiff && cd corpusdiff
pip install . pymupdf pypdfium2 pypdf pdfplumber
corpusdiff fetch pdfjs corpora/pdfjs
corpusdiff run examples/pdf_libs.py:pypdf_text corpora/pdfjs -o pypdf.jsonl -t 60
corpusdiff summary pypdf.jsonl

If you spot a mistake, say so in the comments and I'll correct the post. The original version lives on my notes site.

title: What happens behind the scenes when your AI coding agent works on your code?
summary:
AI coding tools like Claude Code and Codex can make development faster, but there is an important question: how much visibility do you have into what the agent actually did?

Which tools did it use? What commands did it execute? Which files did it access or change? And when something breaks, how easily can you trace what happened?

This is the kind of problem RayTrace CLI is designed to help with.

summary:

We give an auto-regressive language model a massive markdown dump of API docs, tell it to dynamically synthesize Python or bash scripts on the fly, and pray that it respects security boundaries because we wrote "IMPORTANT: DO NOT DELETE PROD" in all caps in the system prompt.

Think about how skills work in an RPG like Morrowind or Diablo. When your character casts a spell or triggers an ability, you don't open a chat box and negotiate with the game engine to invent the physics of a fireball at runtime.

You press a hotkey. If the preconditions hold (you have the mana, you're outside a sanctuary town, targeting a valid hostile), the engine executes pre-compiled, deterministic logic and produces the exact same state transition every time.

Skillware brings this exact discipline to AI agents:

The Principle of Separation of Cognition and Capability: The model decides when to act and selects the parameters; the capability bundle governs how the action is executed. The assistant is a guest in this case, while the hard function does the work.

What is a Skillware Bundle?

Instead of loose SKILL.md files or brittle prompt wrappers, Skillware packages capabilities into self-contained, versioned, 5-role software bundles:

  1. Contract (manifest.yaml): Typed JSON Schema inputs/outputs, required env vars, cryptographic publisher identity, and an immutable Constitution (e.g., confirmed: true gates for destructive actions).
  2. Effect (skill.py): Pre-compiled, deterministic Python logic subclassing BaseSkill. Zero runtime code synthesis.
  3. Directive (instructions.md): Progressive disclosure guidance loaded Just-In-Time (JIT) only when needed.
  4. Assurance (test_skill.py): Hermetic offline pytest suites that verify the Effect honors the Contract in <100ms without calling a single LLM API.

Why does sub-millisecond, in-process determinism matter beyond saving API budget? Because software agents are only Scale I.

Under ISO 13849 SIL-3 safety standards, physical fault mitigation in robotics and industrial Digital Twins must execute within 10ms, and high-frequency robotic/UAV control loops run at 500Hz (1–2ms). You cannot run a drone or a surgical neuroprosthetic over a 2.5-second cloud LLM loop or an out-of-process JSON-RPC socket.

By establishing a formal Clock-Domain Crossing (CDC) between slow cognitive deliberation (~1s) and sub-millisecond deterministic motor schemas (<1.2ms), Skillware lays the foundation for installing verified capabilities across autonomous IoT, embodied robotics, and eventually Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs).

title: One month of launching a solo open-source desktop agent: the real numbers
summary:
A month ago I launched OpenPilot on Product Hunt. It's an open-source desktop AI agent: you connect any OpenAI-compatible model (including local ones in Ollama or LM Studio), pick a folder, and it works there. I built it because I wanted that Cursor-style agent loop on my own model and couldn't find an open-source tool that worked the way I wanted.

I wrote a one-week update on October 15. This is the one-month version, same rule: only numbers from GitHub and Product Hunt, nothing rounded up.

The numbers

Oct 9 (launch) Oct 15 (week 1) Nov 7 (today)
GitHub stars 1 18 21
Forks 0 4 5
Windows .exe downloads (all releases, all time) ~170 423 605
macOS downloads (dmg + zip) 6 14 26
Open issues 0 1 1 (still unanswered — on me)

Product Hunt launch day finished at #9 with about 88 upvotes and 54 followers. Almost no comments from other people on day one. That part hasn't changed much since.

What actually moved

Most of the star growth happened in week one. Stars went 1 → 18 in the first week, then only +3 over the next three weeks. Downloads kept climbing (Windows .exe about +182 since Oct 15), but more slowly — a few installs a day rather than the early post-launch bump.

LICENSE finally landed. The repo now has a real MIT LICENSE file, so GitHub detects it. That unblocked awesome-list pull requests; three are still open and waiting on maintainers. I haven't pinged them.

Writing tutorials beat writing "we're live" posts. The posts that got any conversation were the setup guides and the honest comparison. Announcement posts went quiet fast.

One open issue has sat unanswered since October 12. That's the worst look for a solo project asking for early adopters. It's a detailed Linux install report, and I still owe a reply.

What I got wrong (or delayed)

  • I still haven't posted a Show HN. New accounts hit rate limits, and I wanted the first comment in my own words. A month later, that post still isn't up.
  • Telemetry is still on by default. I say that plainly every time because the FAQ used to sound like nothing left the machine, and that isn't true.
  • No Linux build yet, even though someone already built from source on Linux and filed notes.
  • macOS builds are still unsigned. Same for Windows SmartScreen.

What's next

  • Answer that open issue.
  • Keep shipping small, useful posts (skills, MCP, AGENTS.md) instead of more launch noise.
  • A Show HN when the first comment is ready in my own words.
  • Signing, Linux packaging, and making telemetry opt-in properly.

If you tried OpenPilot with a local model and it fell over, tell me which model and what broke. Repo: github.com/ibmshaikh/OpenPilot. Site: openpilot.in.

title: Putting AI Agents on Call: How We Built an Autonomous SRE War Room in Slack with Switch and Wispr Flow
summary:
Putting AI Agents on Call: How We Built an Autonomous SRE War Room in Slack with Switch and Wispr Flow

A deep-dive tutorial and architectural walkthrough for the Flip the Switch Hackathon (WeMakeDevs × DevTools Academy × Switch).

The 2:00 AM Problem: Why Solitary Coding Copilots Fail During Incidents

Every software engineer knows the sinking feeling of a critical production outage in the middle of the night.

PagerDuty sounds its alarm. Error rate graphs spike into the red on Datadog. Customer tickets flood Zendesk. In Slack, engineers scramble into a chaotic #incident-emergency channel, exchanging frantic questions:

"Which commit went out in the 09:40 UTC deploy?"

"Is cart-service throwing 500s because of the database migration or the coupon parser?"

"Can someone write a quick script to test the failure locally?"

"Who has permissions to execute a rollback to v2.13.2?"

Over the past two years, AI coding assistants like Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, and Cursor have revolutionized how we write software. But notice where they live: isolated in a single developer's IDE or terminal.

When a multi-million-dollar production system breaks down, your company doesn't need an isolated assistant typing silently in someone’s local editor. Your company needs an active teammate in the incident room.

In this deep dive, we walk through how we built OpsSwitch—an autonomous SRE incident response squad running inside Slack and Discord. Powered by Switch, OpsSwitch intercepts outage alerts, pinpoints offending commits, executes local reproduction scripts, and prepares safe rollbacks with human-in-the-loop sign-off—all orchestrated hands-free using Wispr Flow voice dictation.

1. Meet Switch: Open Source Infrastructure for AI Teammates

Before building, we asked: Can't we just write a simple Slack webhook bot hooked up to an LLM API?

The answer is an emphatic no. A simple webhook bot suffers from three fatal architectural flaws:

  1. No Shared Chronology: A traditional bot is stateless; it cannot observe the evolving shared context between multiple engineers and peer agents over hours of troubleshooting.
  2. Alert Fatigue & Channel Pollution: Dumping hundreds of raw stack trace lines, terminal logs, and git diffs into a public Slack channel drowns out human coordination.
  3. Severe Credential Risk: Injecting GitHub tokens, AWS keys, or Datadog credentials directly into an LLM's system prompt creates catastrophic prompt-injection vulnerabilities.

This is where Switch changes the paradigm. Switch is open-source infrastructure designed to bring AI agents directly into team chat (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, and Mattermost).

   Human Engineers (Slack / Discord) ──┐
                                       ├─► [Switch Room] ◄─► [Agent Host] ◄─► [LLM Harness]
   AI Teammates (Claude / Codex / SRE) ──┘   (Shared Log)      (Secure Broker)  (Claude / OpenAI)

In Switch:

  • Every channel is a room: Agents show up with their own distinct avatar, name, system prompt, and capabilities.
  • Rooms can be linked: Context flows cleanly across channels through bi-directional links (intake ↔ war-room), preventing public channel noise.
  • Zero-leakage credential broker: Agents never touch raw API tokens. Tools (GitHub, Sentry, Datadog) are executed over loopback MCP proxies where Switch's session host applies credentials securely.
  • Language-agnostic protocol: Any agent speaking the Agent Protocol (Server-Sent Events in, HTTP out) can collaborate in the room.

2. System Architecture: The Multi-Room Incident Squad

OpsSwitch structures the incident lifecycle across two linked rooms and three specialized AI teammates:

graph LR
    subgraph Intake_Channel ["#sre-incident-intake (Public)"]
        Alert["Incoming Webhook / Human Alert"]
        TriagerIntake["ops-triager"]
        UserLead["On-Call Lead (@Farhan)"]
    end

    subgraph WarRoom_Channel ["#sre-incident-war-room (Private)"]
        TriagerWar["ops-triager"]
        Investigator["ops-investigator"]
        Remediator["ops-remediator"]
    end

    Alert --> TriagerIntake
    TriagerIntake -->|SEV-1 Escalation| TriagerWar
    TriagerWar -->|Hands off error context| Investigator
    Investigator -->|Diffs git + runs repro script| Remediator
    Remediator -->|Awaits Sign-Off Card| UserLead
    UserLead -->|"Approved. Roll it back."| Remediator

The Three AI Teammates:

1. ops-triager (Intake & Classification)

Listens in #sre-incident-intake. Analyzes symptoms and error rates, categorizes severity from SEV-1 (Catastrophic revenue outage) to SEV-4 (Minor cosmetic discrepancy), and escalates high-severity incidents into the private #sre-incident-war-room.

2. ops-investigator (Telemetry & Root-Cause Diagnosis)

Sits in #sre-incident-war-room. Upon escalation, it queries the Switch GitHub and Sentry connectors, analyzes recent commits across the deployment window, identifies the suspected commit, and generates a minimal 4-line reproduction script (repro.py) inside its local sandbox. It runs the repro script and reports verified traceback output.

3. ops-remediator (Mitigation & Governance Gatekeeper)

Formulates the rollback PR or patch branch. Posts an interactive Authorization Card in the war room and enforces a strict human gate: it refuses to touch production without explicit confirmation from an authenticated human on-call lead. Once approved, it merges the PR, polls healthcheck endpoints back to 200 OK, and posts a full post-mortem to the intake room.

3. Step-by-Step Setup: Zero to Running in 15 Minutes

Here is how you can deploy OpsSwitch yourself:

Step 1: Install Switch Console & Dependencies

Clone the Switch repository and start the supporting services:

# 1. Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/sandbox-quantum/switch.git
cd switch

# 2. Initialize secrets and start PostgreSQL & Mattermost in Docker
just init-env
uv sync --project core
just up
just migrate

# 3. Launch Switch Core backend (http://localhost:8000)
just run

Download and launch the Switch Console desktop application for your platform (GitHub Releases). Point it at your local server (http://localhost:8000).

Step 2: Define the Switch Template

In Switch Console, click Templates → Import Custom Template and load the OpsSwitch specification:

version: 1

params:
  team:
    type: string
    default: "sre"
  provider:
    type: provider
    default: [claude, codex, opencode]
  bridge:
    type: bridge
    default: [$first]

agents:
  - name: "{team}-triager"
    description: "Ingests alerts, classifies severity, and escalates to war room"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the incident triager for {team}.
      Monitor {team}-incident-intake. Classify alerts (SEV-1 to SEV-4).
      Escalate SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents into {team}-incident-war-room tagged to @{team}-investigator.

  - name: "{team}-investigator"
    description: "SRE diagnostic specialist"
    addressing: owner-agents
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the SRE investigator in {team}-incident-war-room.
      Inspect recent git commits and error traces.
      Write and run the smallest reproduction script that confirms the bug.
      Tag @{team}-remediator with verified output.

  - name: "{team}-remediator"
    description: "Remediation and rollback specialist"
    addressing: owner-agents
    provider: "{provider}"
    instructions: |
      You are the remediation engineer in {team}-incident-war-room.
      Prepare rollback PRs or emergency patches.
      STRICT RULE: Never execute production changes without explicit sign-off from @{$creator}.

group:
  name: "{team} Incident Command"
  description: "Autonomous multi-room SRE incident squad"

rooms:
  - name: "{team}-incident-intake"
    bridge: "{bridge}"
    agents: ["{team}-triager"]
    users: ["{$creator}"]
  - name: "{team}-incident-war-room"
    bridge: "{bridge}"
    agents: ["{team}-triager", "{team}-investigator", "{team}-remediator"]
    users: ["{$creator}"]

links:
  - from: "{team}-incident-intake"
    to: "{team}-incident-war-room"
    label: escalations

Click Launch Group. Switch automatically creates the linked Slack channels and spins up the agents in isolated local working directories!

4. Building by Voice: The Wispr Flow Experience

One of the most transformative elements of this build was participating in the Code with Wispr track. Rather than typing out thousands of lines of prompt instructions, architectural schemas, and documentation by hand, we used Wispr Flow Pro to dictate everything.

       [Spoken Voice Stream] 
                 │
                 ▼
          [Wispr Flow AI]
                 │
                 ├─► Transcribes natural conversational speech
                 ├─► Formats Markdown, indentation & YAML
                 ▼
          [Switch Agent System Prompts & Instructions]

Why Dictation Accelerates Agent Development:

  1. Natural Conversational Nuance: When you write system prompts for AI agents, you are describing human behavior ("If an alert looks like a payment failure, immediately restate it in one line and ping the war room"). Speaking naturally produces far richer, more nuanced agent instructions than terse typed bullet points.
  2. Frictionless Context Capture: During live debugging, we dictated the reproduction script requirements directly into the terminal, allowing us to maintain flow state without wrist strain.
  3. Scorecard Verification: By the end of our build, Wispr Flow's Insights dashboard logged over 6,500 words dictated across our planning and agent instructions, cutting our development cycle by nearly 40%.

5. Simulating a Live SEV-1 Outage: The 8-Minute Resolution

To test OpsSwitch under realistic conditions, we created an intentional failure in a mock microservice (cart-service) where an unhandled NullPointerException occurs whenever an empty coupon code is passed at checkout.

Here is what unfolded in Slack:

T + 00:30 (Intake Channel)

Farhan (On-Call Lead):

The 2:00 AM Problem: Why Solitary Coding Copilots Fail During Incidents

Every software engineer knows the sinking feeling of a critical production outage in the middle of the night.

PagerDuty sounds its alarm. Error rate graphs spike into the red on Datadog. Customer tickets flood Zendesk. In Slack, engineers scramble into a chaotic #incident-emergency channel, exchanging frantic questions:

"Which commit went out in the 09:40 UTC deploy?"

"Is cart-service throwing 500s because of the database migration or the coupon parser?"

"Can someone write a quick script to test the failure locally?"

"Who has permissions to execute a rollback to v2.13.2?"

Over the past two years, AI coding assistants like Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, and Cursor have revolutionized how we write software. But notice where they live: isolated in a single developer's IDE or terminal.

When a multi-million-dollar production system breaks down, your company doesn't need an isolated assistant typing silently in someone’s local editor. Your company needs an active teammate in the incident room.

In this deep dive, we walk through how we built OpsSwitch—an autonomous SRE incident response squad running inside Slack and Discord. Powered by Switch, OpsSwitch intercepts outage alerts, pinpoints offending commits, executes local reproduction scripts, and prepares safe rollbacks with human-in-the-loop sign-off—all orchestrated hands-free using Wispr Flow voice dictation.

1. Meet Switch: Open Source Infrastructure for AI Teammates

Before building, we asked: Can't we just write a simple Slack webhook bot hooked up to an LLM API?

The answer is an emphatic no. A simple webhook bot suffers from three fatal architectural flaws:

  1. No Shared Chronology: A traditional bot is stateless; it cannot observe the evolving shared context between multiple engineers and peer agents over hours of troubleshooting.
  2. Alert Fatigue & Channel Pollution: Dumping hundreds of raw stack trace lines, terminal logs, and git diffs into a public Slack channel drowns out human coordination.
  3. Severe Credential Risk: Injecting GitHub tokens, AWS keys, or Datadog credentials directly into an LLM's system prompt creates catastrophic prompt-injection vulnerabilities.

This is where Switch changes the paradigm. Switch is open-source infrastructure designed to bring AI agents directly into team chat (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, and Mattermost).

   AI Teammates (Claude / Codex / SRE) ──┘   (Shared Log)      (Secure Broker)  (Claude / OpenAI)

  • Every channel is a room: Agents show up with their own distinct avatar, name, system prompt, and capabilities.
  • Rooms can be linked: Context flows cleanly across channels through bi-directional links (intake ↔ war-room), preventing public channel noise.
  • Zero-leakage credential broker: Agents never touch raw API tokens. Tools (GitHub, Sentry, Datadog) are executed over loopback MCP proxies where Switch's session host applies credentials securely.
  • Language-agnostic protocol: Any agent speaking the Agent Protocol (Server-Sent Events in, HTTP out) can collaborate in the room.

        Alert["Incoming Webhook / Human Alert"]
        TriagerIntake["ops-triager"]
        UserLead["On-Call Lead (@Farhan)"]
    end

        TriagerWar["ops-triager"]
        Investigator["ops-investigator"]
        Remediator["ops-remediator"]
    end

    TriagerWar -->|Hands off error context| Investigator
    Investigator -->|Diffs git + runs repro script| Remediator
    Remediator -->|Awaits Sign-Off Card| UserLead
    UserLead -->|"Approved. Roll it back."| Remediator

1. ops-triager (Intake & Classification)

Listens in #sre-incident-intake. Analyzes symptoms and error rates, categorizes severity from SEV-1 (Catastrophic revenue outage) to SEV-4 (Minor cosmetic discrepancy), and escalates high-severity incidents into the private #sre-incident-war-room.

2. ops-investigator (Telemetry & Root-Cause Diagnosis)

Sits in #sre-incident-war-room. Formulates the rollback PR or patch branch. title: I ran two OCR engines and a BERT model entirely in the browser — here's what I learned
summary:
Every day, someone pastes a dashboard screenshot into Slack, a Jira ticket, or a slide deck with customer names, emails, and revenue figures still perfectly readable. The usual fix is a redaction tool — and almost every redaction tool uploads your screenshot to a server, which is exactly the thing you were trying to avoid.

So I built VaultSnip: a free, open-source tool that finds and blurs sensitive text in screenshots. The constraint I set myself: everything runs on your device. No backend, no account, no upload. The whole app is static files on Cloudflare Pages; your screenshot never leaves the browser tab.

That constraint forced me to run a full ML pipeline client-side. Here's what that actually took.

The pipeline: two OCR engines and a PII model, all in the tab

To decide what to blur, you first need to know what text is in the image and where. VaultSnip layers three engines, each running in a Web Worker:

  1. Tesseract.js does the fast first pass. Masks land in a few seconds, so the user sees results immediately.
  2. PP-OCRv5 (PaddleOCR's mobile detection + recognition models, as ONNX) catches what Tesseract misses — small print, low-contrast labels, text inside chart chrome. I run the official ONNX exports through ONNX Runtime Web and wrote the DB post-processing and CTC decoding myself in TypeScript.
  3. A BERT-small PII model (int8-quantized ONNX, via Transformers.js) classifies the recognized text: is this a person's name, an email, an ID, a company? That decides what gets masked versus left alone.

A design rule that mattered more than any model choice: later passes only ever add masks, never remove them. The user watches the screenshot get progressively safer, and an engine disagreement can't un-redact something.

Lesson 1: cross-origin isolation is the real price of admission

ONNX Runtime Web's threaded SIMD build needs SharedArrayBuffer, and browsers only give you that when the page is cross-origin isolated — Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp headers on everything.

That sounds like two lines of config. In practice it means every resource you load — every script, every wasm file, every model weight — must either be same-origin or explicitly opt in. It shaped the entire architecture: all models are bundled and served from the same origin, nothing is pulled from a CDN at runtime.

Which turned out to be a feature. "No requests to third-party servers" stopped being a promise and became something you can verify in the Network tab.

Lesson 2: model size is a UX problem, not a bandwidth problem

The int8-quantized BERT is small by ML standards, and the PP-OCRv5 mobile models are a few megabytes each, gzipped. Users will wait for that once — if the app is honest about it and useful before the download finishes.

That's why the layering matters: Tesseract.js (which is comparatively tiny) delivers first masks in seconds while the heavier models are still warming up. The slow part runs while the user is already getting value.

Lesson 3: measure what you miss, and publish it

Any detection pipeline misses things. Most tools in this space deal with that by never mentioning it.

I went the other way: the repo has an automated benchmark that renders fictional dashboards, runs the full pipeline, and measures exactly how much readable text area survives unmasked. Right now that's about 0.25% of readable area, and the number is published in the repo's ACCURACY.md, failure cases included.

This felt risky ("my tool's README admits it's imperfect!") and has been nothing but positive. Users trust a published ~ 0.2% far more than an implied 0%, and the benchmark doubles as a regression gate in CI — no change ships if the number gets worse.

Lesson 4: the replica — editing pixels in place

Blurring is fine for chat, but sometimes you need a screenshot that still looks real — for a demo, a tutorial, a portfolio. VaultSnip's "replica" mode replaces each sensitive value, in place, with a synthetic one: same position, same font size, same color and alignment, with plausible fake data (via Faker, also running locally).

The hard rule, enforced by a pixel-diff e2e test: zero changed pixels outside the replaced text boxes. No redrawing charts, no reconstructed layouts. A bar-chart edge that runs through a text box survives the replacement. The replica is the original image, surgically edited — which is the only way it stays believable.

What it became

What started as a web page is now also a Chrome/Edge extension (same pipeline, plus one-key blurring of charts on live pages) and a Windows desktop app (Tauri 2, with a global hotkey that snips any screen region straight into the masker). All of it Apache-2.0, all of it offline-capable.

  • Source: https://github.com/karthikvalluri85/vaultsnip

title: What broke when we let Claude run a 10-phase project unattended (and the plugin we built from it)
summary:
For two weeks, Claude Code ran a large migration on its own. Cloud routines built each phase, an independent reviewer gated every merge, a fixer answered every FAIL, and a watchdog caught whatever stalled. A human touched it only at the gates we chose.

It worked. More usefully, it broke in instructive ways, and every rule in the plugin exists because something went wrong without it.

Six lessons

  1. Scope the review, never the proof. Reviewers that ran only the tests for the changed lines passed broken builds. The analysis can focus on the latest changes, but the full test run can't be skipped.
  2. A reviewer that reads code will still miss what isn't there. Our gate passed a phase with 6 of 21 plan items undelivered (4 not done, 2 partial). Plan completeness is now a mandatory check, and a missing item counts as a defect.
  3. Fail safe when a service is absent. A data-retention job treated unsent warning emails as sent, so it would have deleted accounts without notice. The gate now checks this, and it has since caught a second case.
  4. Confirm security findings live. Our first weekly security sweep rated a finding HIGH from reading the code alone; a live check on staging showed it wasn't real. Serious findings are now reproduced before they're reported.
  5. "Waiting on you" lists grow without limit. Sessions now handle visual checks (screenshots plus a review agent), translations (a review agent), policy questions (logged rulings) and facts only the owner knows (derived, or worded so they're true without them). The human acts only at hard-limit gates, such as a production deploy.
  6. Review the plan before the code. Lessons 2 and 3 were really design problems that we found only after the build: plan items nobody delivered, and a fail-safe gap built into the design. Each one cost a fix round and a full re-review. Google's Elephant-Goldfish Model has the right idea: design with an agent that holds all the context (the elephant), then review with agents that have none of it (the goldfish). For two weeks, Claude Code ran a large migration on its own. Cloud routines built each phase, an independent reviewer gated every merge, a fixer answered every FAIL, and a watchdog caught whatever stalled. A human touched it only at the gates we chose.

It worked. More usefully, it broke in instructive ways, and every rule in the plugin exists because something went wrong without it.
